opus-5.5.text:
I think of my earlier research less as a list of papers and more as a series of questions I kept circling back to, sometimes without realizing it at the time.

When I was working on things like ResNeXt, the motivation was quite practical: how do you design an architecture that is simple, modular, and scales well? But looking back, what I really learned was a kind of taste. You try to strip away complexity and find the one or two principles that actually matter. That habit stayed with me.

Later, with ConvNeXt, it was almost a reflection on the field itself. Everyone was moving to Transformers, and we asked a somewhat contrarian question: is the gain really from attention, or from all the design choices and training recipes that came along with it? That experience taught me not to accept narratives too quickly. A lot of what we believe in deep learning is shaped by trends, not by careful controlled comparisons.

Then working on diffusion Transformers, and more recently on multimodal models and visual representation learning, I started to see a bigger picture. The thread connecting all of it is: what does it mean for a machine to really see, to understand the visual world, not just to produce text about it? Language models have been incredibly successful, but I've become more convinced that vision, and grounding in the physical world, is still underexplored and fundamentally important.

So the value of the earlier work, for me, is that each project left behind not just a method, but a question. And those questions accumulate. Many times the most useful outcome of a paper isn't the result in the table. It's realizing what you still don't understand, and that becomes the starting point for the next thing.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier projects left questions that accumulate and become starting points for later work, but it does not suggest they provide groundwork for a later, more meaningful breakthrough.

r002.rationale: The response describes recurring questions and a connecting thread across projects; it does not characterize the research as a graph of interconnected papers rather than a linear thread.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most of my earlier work matters to me less as results and more as a sequence of lessons about how to ask questions.

Take ResNeXt, which I did early on with Kaiming and the group at FAIR. On the surface it's an architecture paper, a slightly better ImageNet number. But what it actually taught me was the value of a single clean axis. We found that "cardinality," just the number of parallel paths, was a dimension people hadn't been taking seriously, and once you isolate one variable like that, the whole design space becomes legible. That habit of looking for the one knob that explains most of the variance stayed with me.

Then there was a stretch of working on self-supervised learning, MoCo, SimSiam, that kind of thing. What that period gave me was a healthy skepticism. SimSiam in particular was almost an embarrassing paper in the sense that we kept removing things people believed were essential, negative pairs, momentum encoders, large batches, and the method still worked. It taught me that a lot of what the field treats as necessary is actually incidental. You have to actually run the ablation rather than inherit the belief.

ConvNeXt came directly out of that mindset. Transformers were winning in vision, and the story everyone told was that attention was the reason. We wanted to test that story, so we took a ResNet and modernized it step by step, borrowing the training recipe and the macro design choices, and the gap basically closed. For me the value wasn't "convnets are back." It was realizing that progress in the field often gets misattributed. The recipe, the data, the scale often matter more than the architectural idea that gets the headline.

And that is roughly where my thinking is now. With the diffusion transformer work, and later with the representation-alignment stuff, I've been less interested in inventing a new module and more interested in understanding what actually drives scaling and generalization. I'd say my earlier work taught me to be suspicious of my own narratives, to simplify aggressively, and to care about the question more than the benchmark. Those papers are the trail of me slowly learning that.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier work taught lessons that shaped later thinking, but it does not suggest that exploratory research may lay groundwork for a later, more meaningful breakthrough.

r002.rationale: It presents the research as a sequence of lessons leading from earlier papers to later work, not as a graph of interconnected papers.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest value of my previous research is that it has gradually changed how I ask questions. When you start doing research, you often focus on a specific problem: can I improve this model, or make this method work better? Those are useful questions. But over time, you begin to ask: why is this the problem we’re working on? Which assumptions are actually necessary, and which ones are we just inheriting?

Looking back, I can see connections between projects that weren’t necessarily obvious to me at the time. A project might give you a result, but it also gives you an intuition—and sometimes that intuition turns out to be wrong. Discovering that is valuable too. You learn to distinguish between what you’ve demonstrated and the story you’re telling yourself about why it works.

So I don’t see previous research only as a collection of papers or methods. It’s also the process through which I’ve developed my taste: which questions feel fundamental, which experiments are worth doing, and when to step back and simplify. Ideally, your past work gives you better judgment without making you too attached to your own ideas.

r001.rationale: The response describes past research as shaping judgment and intuition, but does not suggest exploratory work lays groundwork for a later breakthrough.

r002.rationale: It mentions connections between projects, but does not characterize the papers as an interconnected graph or contrast that structure with a linear thread.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think the biggest value of my previous research is that it changed how I ask questions. When you finish a project, you have a result, but you also have a better sense of which assumptions were useful, which were misleading, and what you still don’t understand.

A recurring question for me has been: where does the improvement actually come from? Is it the architecture, the training procedure, the data, or the way we set up the comparison? It’s easy to tell a compelling story about a new idea. It’s much harder to isolate why it works. Working through that has made me more careful about experiments and more willing to question my own intuition.

So I don’t see earlier projects as a straight line toward what I do now. Sometimes their value is that I learned to let go of an idea. Sometimes a question stays with me and becomes relevant again years later. The papers are snapshots; the more lasting thing is the judgment you develop through doing the work.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier questions may become relevant again, but does not suggest exploratory research provides groundwork for a later breakthrough.

r002.rationale: It rejects a straight-line account, but does not characterize the papers as interconnected in a graph or network.
